The purpose of this document is to outline the District of Columbia’s (D.C. or the District) plan for providing assistance to families with children using funds provided under Title I of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) of 1996 (Pub. L. No. 104-193), and the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Final Rules published in the Federal Register on April 12, 1999. The Act amends Section 402 of the Social Security Act to require that states submit a plan to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) that outlines how the state will provide TANF benefits.

The District uses federal, MOE/Separate State Program, and Solely State Funded (SSF) funds to operate a cash assistance program and provide supportive services for families with children through the District’s TANF program. The District does not commingle funding streams. The local legal authority for this program is the District of Columbia Public Assistance Act of 1982 (D.C. Law § 4-101; D.C. Official Code § 4-201.01, et seq.), as amended. The provisions of this Plan are effective October 1, 2023. The District’s Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program provides cash assistance to eligible families with a suite of services to facilitate their path to success. These services include access to resources that can be bundled together to meet the family’s individual needs. The District employs a Two-Generation (2Gen) Approach to reaching and serving families so children and parents can rise together.

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

In Fiscal Year (FY) 2016, the District of Columbia (D.C.) Department of Human Services (DHS) revised its TANF Employment & Education Program (TEP) to better align with the growing national trend of incorporating a multi-generational (2Gen) approach to serving TANF customers and their families. DHS has since integrated the six (6) nationally recognized pillars of this 2 Gen approach (Economic Assets, Social Capital, Health, including Mental Health, Post-Secondary and Employment Pathways, and Early Childhood Education,

Bowser, DHS convened a TANF Hardship Working Group that recommended a Hardship Extension Policy for customers who received TANF in D.C. for 60 months or longer. The TANF Hardship Working Group included DHS staff, local advocacy organizations, members and staff of the D.C. Council, TEP providers, and, most importantly, TANF customers. The working group addressed the impending TANF policy change calling for a termination of TANF cash assistance benefits, in October 2017, for customers who had reached the Federal lifetime limit of 60-months of TANF benefit receipt.

The culmination of both activities led to the development of the current TANF Policy that took effect April 1, 2018 along with revisions to the TEP service delivery model that took effect on October 1, 2018. The new TANF Policy in D.C. has accomplished three critical goals:

1. Rescinded the plan to terminate benefits at 60+ months, allowing D.C. residents access to cash assistance and employment, education, and 2Gen services as long as they continue to meet TANF eligibility requirements;

2. Cash Assistance Program - Elevated the TANF benefit amount for 60+ month customers who had experienced cash reductions in benefits since 2011 via the previous TANF policy; and

3. Embraced the value that puts families, and most importantly children, first enacting a two-part TANF work sanction policy: a. Bifurcating the monthly TANF benefit, allocating 80% of the benefit for child protection and enrichment, and 20% for parental engagement in employment, education, and 2Gen services; and

The TANF program also provides an opportunity for families to engage in services that support their capacity to earn a living wage. All the provisions of the D.C. TANF program are intended to meet one or more of the following basic purposes of TANF as articulated in the Federal statute and regulation:

1) Provide assistance to needy families so that children may be cared for in their own homes or in the homes of relatives;

2) End the dependence of needy parents on government benefits by promoting job preparation, work, and marriage;

3) Prevent and reduce the incidence of out-of-wedlock pregnancies and establish annual numerical goals for preventing and reducing the incidence of these pregnancies; and

4) Encourage the formation and maintenance of two-parent families. SECTION 2: PLAN OVERVIEW Program Goals

D.C.’s TANF plan fits within the broader key priorities for its residents, which include:

Create pathways to the middle class for residents by 1) Adopting a Two Generation (2-Gen) approach that values children’s enrichment, security, and well-being and the entire family’s welfare.

b) Through an integrated economic security and housing stability model, develop an effective system of care for families who experience homelessness to prevent homelessness, provide shelter to those who need it, and support families on a faster and more stable path out of homelessness.

Fundamentally, D.C. has designed a TANF program which recognizes that each individual and each family are unique and that services should be adapted to their specific circumstances, conditions, and needs in order for them to achieve their personal goals. As such, D.C. has created a TANF program which is tailored to the individual needs of each family. The goal of the program is to help families achieve a pathway to the middle class by realizing their own aspirations.

Decreased Case Manager-to-Customer caseload sizes to allow for more in-depth case coaching opportunities; and 5. The inclusion of six (6) nationally recognized 2Gen activities programmed into DHS’s case management and invoicing system to allow for tracking of customer participation in each activity.

D.C. seeks to continuously improve and increase the types of service-delivery options available to customers by:

1. Modify the timing of the referral process to providers, based on the presenting needs, as defined by each individual customer.

2. D.C. is revising its Work Verification Plan based on ongoing program and policy changes made over the last several years. DHS seeks to simplify the work verification process to reduce the burden to both customers and providers to the extent possible under federal law.

3. Deployed new TANF Assessment Tool – In May 2022, DHS made several changes to its TANF assessment including applying a person-centered, full-frame lens, along with a strengths-based approach that more accurately identify how DHS can best serve the whole family, both parent and child(ren), in the most respectful and productive way. The DHS Assessment Portal (DAP) has modernized DHS-ESA’s traditional assessment process by providing a web-based application that is accessible to staff and customers. • DAP uses a customer-centered approach that focuses on the customer’s priorities and strengths. DAP examines the needs of the whole family by asking questions that use a 2- Gen lens, including referrals to outside services and additional supports. • DHS wants to make the assessment process for benefits meaningful and accessible for customers. The Customer Assessment Portal (CAP) allows customers to complete the assessment, which is a requirement for TANF eligibility, on their own time. CAP helps DHS learn more about a customer’s needs and the needs of their family to provide supportive services and offer resources.

TANF Program Service Delivery Options In addition to funding basic cash assistance and employment and training programs for TANF recipients, D.C. uses or intends to use federal TANF or MOE Separate State funds for the following activities for TANF-eligible families (for programs and services other than cash assistance, D.C. has eligibility criteria of under 300% of the Federal Poverty Level):

1. Employment, educational, and support service offerings developed through a multigenerational framework: a. Job Placement (JP) Service Providers help customers navigate and engage in purposeful career exploration to identify the customer’s preferred work industry and career pathway. Together, the customer and Case Manager work collaboratively to create a series of detailed Individual Responsibility Plans (dIRPs) that document the iterative steps and activities the customer will pursue to meet their employment goals. This falls under TANF purpose #3 and is not considered assistance.

b. Education & Occupational Training (EOT) Service Providers assist customers to navigate and enroll in education programs that lead to nationally recognized certifications and credentials. The EOT incentive structure recognizes education and occupational training enrollment, maintenance, and completion. Programs may include, but are not limited to, linkage to adult education and vocational educational training, programs that provide fast-track GED exam in 10 weeks or less, English as a Second Language programs, and family literacy programs. Identification, Screening and Assessment Participants are screened for domestic violence at numerous stages in the process, by various entities, in writing and in person, to effectively capture persons suffering from domestic violence. First, DHS itself screens for domestic violence at both its intake and recertification applications. Additionally, DHS administers the Economic Security Comprehensive Assessment to assess and identify whether TANF applicants face barriers to employment or participation in the program, including domestic violence, sexual harassment, sexual assault, and stalking. If current or historic evidence of domestic violence, sexual harassment, sexual assault, and stalking is identified, a referral for additional screening or assessment services will be provided to the applicant or recipient who should comply with the instructions. The additional screening is completed by a domestic violence provider in D.C., trained in the nature and dynamics of sexual harassment and domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking. If an entity that operates a TANF work or education program discovers that a recipient has a domestic violence, sexual harassment, sexual assault, or stalking issue and may need services, that entity may contact DHS and a referral to the domestic violence service providers(s) will be made at that time. The domestic violence service provider will determine the right course of action for the family, e.g., shelter/alternate housing, counseling services, legal options, etc., on a case-by-case basis.

The District of Columbia will operate a program to provide Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) so that the children may be cared for in their own homes or in homes of relatives or caregivers and to end dependence of needy able-bodied adults on government benefits by promoting job preparation, work and pathway to the middle class.
